en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on the Power of Psychic Potency.
9. The Question on Further Duties “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:

‘Whatever was to be done by the Tathāgata, all that was fully accomplished at the very foot of the Bodhi tree; there is nothing further to be done by the Tathāgata, nor is there any need for the adding of what has already been done. Yet this three-month period of seclusion is observed. How is this?”
“If, venerable Nāgasena, whatever was to be done by the Tathāgata was all brought to completion at the very foot of the Bodhi tree,
and there was nothing further for the Tathāgata to do nor any need to add to what had been done,
then the statement that he remained in seclusion for three months is false.”

If he has been in seclusion for three months, then the statement, “Whatever was to be done by the Tathāgata, all that was brought to completion at the foot of the Bodhi tree,” would also be false. There is no need for seclusion for one who has completed what was to be done;
it is only for one who still has work to do that there is seclusion—just as medicine is required only for one who is ill, for what need is there for medicine for one who is not ill?
Just as food is required only for one who is hungry, for what need is there for food for one who is not hungry?
“In the same way, venerable Nāgasena, there is no seclusion for one who has completed what was to be done; seclusion belongs only to one who still has work to do.
This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Whatever was to be done by the Tathāgata, O Great King, all of that was brought to final completion at the very foot of the Bodhi tree.”
There is nothing further for the Tathāgata to do, nor is there any need to augment what has already been accomplished. The Blessed One has been in seclusion for three months.

Seclusion, Great King, possesses many virtues; indeed, all Tathāgatas have attained omniscience after practicing seclusion, and thus, recollecting the merit of their own well-performed deeds, they resort to seclusion.
Just as, Great King, a man who has received a boon from a king and obtained wealth remembers the merit of that well-done deed and attends upon the king again and again;
even so, Great King, all the Tathāgatas, having attained omniscience after secluding themselves, resort to seclusion while remembering the merit of that well-done deed.

Or again, Great King, just as a man who is sick, suffering, and gravely ill, having attended upon a physician and recovered his health, remembers that well-performed service and attends upon the physician again and again;
even so, Great King, all the Tathāgatas, having attained omniscience after secluding themselves, practice seclusion while recollecting those well-performed qualities.
Moreover, Great King, there are these twenty-eight qualities of seclusion, recollecting which the Tathāgatas practice seclusion.
Which twenty-eight? Here, Great King,
when one who is in seclusion practices seclusion, he protects himself, increases his lifespan,
bestows strength, covers over faults, removes ill-repute, brings about renown, dispels discontent, and establishes delight.
It removes fear, produces self-confidence, removes indolence, generates energy,
removes lust, removes hatred, removes delusion, destroys conceit, breaks down discursive thought, makes the mind one-pointed,
moistens the mind, engenders joy, creates reverence, and brings about gain; it makes one worthy of homage.
It brings about rapture, it produces gladness, it reveals the true nature of conditioned phenomena,
it uproots rebirth in existence,
and it bestows the fruit of all asceticism. These, O Great King, are the twenty-eight qualities of seclusion, recollecting which the Tathāgatas cultivate seclusion.
Moreover, Great King, the Tathāgatas, having fulfilled their intentions, resort to seclusion because they desire to experience the bliss of the attainment of peace.
Great King, there are four reasons why the Tathāgatas resort to seclusion.
What are these four?
Great King, the Tathāgatas resort to seclusion for the sake of comfort in their dwelling; the Tathāgatas resort to seclusion for the abundance of blameless qualities;
the Tathāgatas resort to seclusion because it is the path of all the Noble Ones;
and the Tathāgatas resort to seclusion because it has been praised, extolled, and lauded by all the Buddhas.
“By these four reasons, Great King, do the Tathāgatas resort to seclusion.

Thus, Great King, it is not out of a sense of duty, nor for the sake of increasing what has already been done, but rather because they perceive the excellence of its qualities that the Tathāgatas resort to seclusion.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! So it is; thus do I accept it.”
The ninth question: On Further Duties.
